content.title: Dougherty: At 2026 Masters, Justin Rose seeks his 1st green jacket
content.text: Justin Rose plays a stroke from a bunker on the No. 2 hole during a practice round prior to the Masters at Augusta National Golf Club, Monday, April 6, 2026.Augusta National/Augusta National/Getty ImagesEditor’s note: This column originally ran this past Tuesday. On Sunday at the Masters, Justin Rose is currently in contention.AUGUSTA, Ga. — Mastering Thursdays at Augusta National hasn’t been the problem for Justin Rose. He has held or shared the first-round lead at the Masters a record five times.Article continues below this adGet Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.Get Digital Access and Stay Informed With Trusted Local News.ONLY 25¢None of those early advantages has led to donning a green jacket the subsequent Sunday, but he is getting closer. Rose, whose lone major championship came in the 2013 U.S. Open, lost in a playoff last year to fellow European Rory McIlroy, who finally broke his Masters maiden.At 45, Rose knows that he is nearing the end of the garden. He will begin play Thursday in his 21st Masters, appreciating that his name appears on the trophy three times as the runner-up.“I've pretty much done what it takes to win,” Rose said. “I just haven't walked over the line.”Make the Times Union a Preferred Source on Google to see more of our journalism when you search.Add Preferred SourceLet’s start near the beginning. As an amateur at age 17, he tied for fourth at the 1998 British Open. He then turned professional and missed the cut in 21 consecutive tournaments.Article continues below this adIn 2004, at his second Masters, he led the field with a first-round 67. He shot himself out of contention with an 81 on Saturday and tied for 22nd. After failing to qualify the next two years, he shared the Thursday lead in 2007 before posting back-to-back 75s, settling into a tie for fifth. The next year he was tied again after an opening-round 68, then shot 78-73-76 to finish in a tie for 36th. In 2021 he started with a leading 65 but fell to seventh. Rose was on top last year with a first-day 65. A third-round 75 nearly took him out of it, but a final-round 66 tied him with McIlroy.“If I look back at my career, I probably learned the hard way,” Rose said. “Twenty-one missed cuts suggests I didn't learn very quickly and could have asked a few more questions.”In his Masters career, Rose has averaged 70.5 on Thursdays, 72.7 on Fridays, 72.5 on Saturdays and 71.4 on Sundays. He has seven career top-10s but still isn’t invited to the Champions Dinner.Article continues below this ad“There was a tendency early in my career to try to be perfect for Thursday,” he said. “Yeah, you need to be ready for Thursday, but you need to save your gas for Sunday, as well.”His growth and maturity were on display in last year’s final round, when he carded 10 birdies en route to a 66 to put pressure on McIlroy, who was playing four groups behind. Instead of looking like a hard-luck runner-up, Rose wore the look of a champion ready to steal the tournament.It turned into quite a duel. McIlroy and Rose shot a best-ball 59, but this wasn’t a member-guest at the local country club. It was Sunday afternoon at Augusta National, where McIlroy prevailed by hitting his approach shot on the first playoff hole to within 3 feet of the pin for birdie.Even in defeat, Rose was lauded for his class and sportsmanship toward his Ryder Cup mate.Article continues below this ad“Justin is a great champion,” McIlroy said after his victory. “I remember watching the playoff of ’17 when he went up against Sergio (Garcia), and that didn’t quite go his way, either, but he’s had a phenomenal record around here, and I feel for him a little bit because he’s been so close.”This year marks the 40th anniversary of Jack Nicklaus’ stirring Masters victory at age 46. Rose is only a year younger than that, but being in the mid-40s in 2026 may be different than in 1986.Rose won his 13th career PGA Tour title in February, shooting a record-breaking 23 under par over 72 holes at Torrey Pines. He was 13th last month at the Players Championship.“A lot of people are wishing me well or thinking it's going to be my year, just based around sentiment,” Rose said. “I'm going to have to manage that a bit this week, and that's going to be part of my week this week — people remembering what happened last year.Article continues below this ad“That's fine, but I've got to be aware of that, be ready for that, and I've got to have my own narrative and not kind of buy into everyone else's narrative.”He has proven he can be a good loser. Rose still hopes he can prove to be a good winner.April 7, 2026|Updated April 12, 2026 8:07 p.m.Pete Dougherty retired from full-time writing in August 2021 after 36 years with the Times Union. He still contributes as a freelance writer on golf and other sports. You can reach him at pete.dougherty7@gmail.com.
